docs.title: About
docs.text:
I am a bioinformatician with a focus on genome evolution, transposable elements, and host–pathogen interactions. My work aims to understand how genome structure, regulatory dynamics, and sequence variation contribute to adaptation and disease at population and species scales.

I have conducted large-scale comparative genomics analyses across multiple rice genomes to study transposable element dynamics and evolutionary patterns, and RNA-seq investigations of fungal pathogenicity to characterize gene expression changes associated with host adaptation. My research integrates statistical modeling, reproducible pipeline development, and high-performance computing to manage and interpret complex genomic datasets.

In parallel, I apply computational structural biology approaches, including molecular docking and molecular dynamics simulations, to investigate protein–ligand interactions and functional mechanisms. Using Python-based workflows built around AutoDock Vina, RDKit, MDAnalysis, and GROMACS, I connect molecular-level modeling with broader genomic and systems-level questions.

I am particularly interested in developing scalable computational frameworks that link genome architecture, evolutionary processes, and functional biology. I aim to advance integrative approaches that combine comparative genomics, transcriptomics, and modeling to address fundamental questions in genome evolution and disease biology.

docs.title: 1. What is Machine Learning?
docs.text:
Machine Learning (ML) is a way to teach computers to learn patterns from data and make decisions without being explicitly programmed for every rule.

Instead of writing:

if marks > 40:
    print("Pass")

We provide data to the computer, and it learns the pattern on its own.

docs.title: 2. Why Do We Need Machine Learning?
2.1. Disease Gene Prediction
docs.text:
• Identify disease-causing mutations

  • Classify variants as benign or pathogenic

  • Predict cancer driver genes

Example: From whole genome sequencing data, ML models can predict whether a mutation is harmful.

docs.title: 2.2. RNA-Seq Expression Analysis
docs.text:
• Cluster genes with similar expression patterns

  • Classify samples (healthy vs diseased)

  • Identify biomarkers

Example: Grouping tumor vs normal samples using gene expression data.

docs.title: 2.3. Crop Disease Prediction
docs.text:
• Detect plant diseases from leaf images

  • Predict resistance genes

  • Classify pathogen strains

Example: Predicting whether a rice plant is infected using image or genomic data.

docs.title: 2.4. Transposon and Genome Annotation
docs.text:
• Identifying transposable elements

  • Classifying repeat families

  • Predicting insertion hotspots

  • Annotating genomes automatically

Example: Classifying unknown repetitive sequences into TE families.

docs.title: 2.5. Protein Structure and Function Prediction
docs.text:
• Predict protein 3D structure

  • Identify functional domains

  • Predict enzyme activity

Example: Predicting protein folding from amino acid sequence.

docs.title: 3. Types of Machine Learning
docs.text:
• Supervised Learning
  • Unsupervised Learning
  • Semi-Supervised Learning
  • Reinforcement Learning

docs.title: What is Supervised Learning?
docs.text:
In supervised learning, the model learns from labeled data.

That means: - We give the computer input data - We also provide the correct output - It learns the relationship between them

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Hours Studied Result

2 Fail 5 Pass 8 Pass

Instead of writing:

if marks > 40:
    print("Pass")

The model learns the rule from data.

docs.title: 1. Classification
docs.text:
Used when the output is a category.

Examples: - Yes / No - Spam / Not Spam - Cat / Dog - Pass / Fail

Classification deals with grouping into categories.

docs.title: Algorithms for Classification
docs.text:
• Logistic Regression
  • Decision Tree
  • K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN)
  • Support Vector Machine (SVM)
  • Kernel SVM
  • Naive Bayes
  • Random Forest

docs.title: 2. Regression
docs.text:
Used when the output is a number.

Examples: - House price prediction - Temperature prediction\ - Predicting exam score

Regression deals only with numerical outputs.

docs.title: Algorithms for Regression
docs.text:
• Linear Regression
  • Multiple Linear Regression
  • Polynomial Regression
  • Support Vector Regression (SVR)
  • Gaussian Process Regression
  • Ridge Regression
  • Lasso Regression
  • Random Forest

docs.title: Example Question
docs.text:
How will the price of a dress be decided?

Possible features: - Brand - Fabric - Size - Season - Demand - Online reviews

If price is a number → Regression problem If price category (Cheap / Medium / Expensive) → Classification problem

docs.title: 2.1 What is Unsupervised Learning?
docs.text:
In unsupervised learning, we provide only input data, but no correct answers.

The model finds patterns by itself.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Suppose we give data about customers:

  • Age
  • Shopping amount
  • Frequency of purchase

The algorithm groups similar customers together. We did not tell it the groups. It discovered them.

docs.title: 2.2 Unsupervised Algorithms
docs.text:
• K-Means Clustering
  • Hierarchical Clustering
  • DBSCAN (Density-Based Spatial Clustering of Applications with Noise)
  • Principal Component Analysis (PCA)
  • Probabilistic clustering (distribution-based clustering)

docs.title: What is Semi-Supervised Learning?
docs.text:
It is a mix of: - A small amount of labeled data - A large amount of unlabeled data

Used when labeling data is expensive or difficult.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Imagine you have: - 1000 medical images - Only 50 are labeled

The model learns from the 50 labeled images and improves using the remaining unlabeled images.

docs.title: Inductive Methods
docs.text:
• Self-training
  • Co-training

docs.title: Transductive and Graph-Based Methods
docs.text:
• Label Propagation
  • Label Spreading

docs.title: Deep Learning Approaches
docs.text:
• Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs)
  • Consistency Regularization
  • Generative Models
  • Semi-Supervised Support Vector Machines (S3VMs)

docs.title: What is Reinforcement Learning?
docs.text:
In Reinforcement Learning (RL), an agent learns by:

  • Taking actions
  • Receiving rewards or penalties
  • Improving over time

It learns through trial and error.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Think of training a game-playing AI.

  • If it wins → reward
  • If it loses → penalty

Over time, it learns the best strategy.

docs.title: Key Terms in Reinforcement Learning
docs.text:
• Agent → The learner
  • Environment → Where the agent acts
  • Action → What the agent does
  • Reward → Feedback received

docs.title: Value-Based
docs.text:
• Q-Learning
  • Deep Q Networks (DQN)
  • Value Iteration

docs.title: Policy-Based
docs.text:
• Policy Gradient Methods
  • REINFORCE (Monte Carlo)
  • Trust Region Policy Optimization (TRPO)

docs.title: Actor-Critic
docs.text:
• Advantage Actor-Critic (A2C)
  • Asynchronous Advantage Actor-Critic (A3C)
  • Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO)
  • Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (DDPG)
  • Soft Actor-Critic (SAC)

docs.title: Other Methods
docs.text:
• Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS)
  • State-Action-Reward-State-Action (SARSA)
  • Dynamic Programming
